paper_title: Let the Fixer Decide: Training a Code Localizer from the Fixer's Likelihood

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Code localizers are usually trained to predict the files a reference patch edits, but the code a fixer needs to read is not the same as the code it changes. We propose Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL): the localizer proposes several localizations, a frozen fixer scores each by how likely it makes a verified patch, and the localizer is trained on these scores with weighted supervised fine-tuning, without running tests and without reinforcement learning. We build the full pipeline on Gemma 4 E4B for the Kaggle Gemma-4 Developer Agent competition, from 1,629 test-verified Kimi K3 trajectories. The FGL target helps the fixer find the bug as often as the teacher's localization while using 27.5% less code. On the development set, one EM round moves the agent in the expected direction compared with a matched control: more tasks reach a patch (53 vs. 46), fewer tasks get stuck reading files that do not exist (43 vs. 54), and more tasks are solved (8 vs. 6). Training also changes how the agent works: trained agents explore about three times more than the base model and write far fewer wrong patches, and the single agent solves up to 11 of 78 tasks, against 8 for the base model. An analysis of 13 evaluation runs identifies what limits a 4B agent under an 8-minute budget (time, repetition loops and edit quality) and gives practical lessons for training small coding agents. All data, code and adapters are publicly available.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Language-model agents now fix many real GitHub issues on benchmarks such as SWE-bench [Jimenez et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024]. Some explore and edit the repository freely with shell tools [Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025]; others first find the relevant code and then write patch [Xia et al., 2024]. When open models are trained for the second design, the localizer learns to predict the locations that the reference patch edits [Xie et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2025]. That label is weak stand-in for what the fixer needs. fix often depends on code it does not change, such as caller, base class or test, and localizer with about 80% file accuracy can still give only 38% resolved issues [Al Mamun & Uddin, 2026]. In retrieval-augmented language models the answer is well known: train the retriever on what helps the reader [Lewis et al., 2020; Sachan et al., 2021; Izacard et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024]. For issue resolution, learning from outcomes has meant reinforcement learning with test execution [Wei et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025], which is expensive. We ask whether localizer can learn from the fixer with supervised fine-tuning alone. https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/gemma-4-developer-agent-paper 1 Fixer-Guided Localization (FGL) treats the localization as hidden variable. The localizer proposes candidates, frozen fixer scores each by the log-probability it gives to verified patch, and the localizer is fine-tuned on the candidates weighted by these scores. This is expectation-maximization (EM) [Dempster et al., 1977]; every update is ordinary weighted fine-tuning, and the only environment is forward pass of the fixer. We built the method for the Kaggle Gemma 4 Developer Agent competition [Markowitz et al., 2026], which fixes the model, the serving stack and the tools. With limited budget we trained only the smallest model, Gemma 4 E4B. The result is mixed, and we report it as it is: the method works offline and moves the agents behaviour in the right direction, but on 78 development tasks no trained system is significantly better than the untrained model. We study 13 evaluation runs to explain why. Contributions. Method. localizer trained from the fixers likelihood of verified patch, with weighted supervised fine-tuning only (Section 2). Data. pipeline that generates and verifies teacher trajectories inside the competitions own agent loop and sandbox , pipeline that converts them into two-agent training data without inventing any tool output, and the released set of 1,629 verified trajectories (Section 3). Evaluation. Eight systems on Gemma 4 E4B, compared with paired tests on the same tasks, including matched control for the EM round (Section 5). Analysis. What limits small agent under strict time budget, with practical lessons for others (Sections 5.3 and 6).

sections.title: 2.1 Two agents
sections.content: One frozen base model carries two LoRA adapters [Hu et al., 2022] (Figure 1). The fixer is the main agent. It calls the localizer as tool; the localizer explores the repository in fresh session and answers with list of at most 8 code locations (path, symbol, line range, and whether the location is to be edited or only read). The fixer reads these locations, may read more code (a request), then edits, tests and submits.

sections.title: 2.2 Localization as a hidden variable

The localizer gives pϕ(z x, R) over localizations z, and the fixer gives pθ(y x, ctx(z)), where ctx(z) is the code that points to. sections.title: 2.3 Scores and weights
sections.content: We draw candidates z1, . . . , zK from the localizer itself. With the localizer as the proposal, the posterior weights become softmax over the fixers scores. We score each candidate by sk = 1 + (cid:88) ty + log pθ (cid:0)y <t, x, ctx(zk)(cid:1) λctx tok(zk) λreq ak, (3) and set wk = softmaxk(sk/τ ). Three choices make this work in practice: Only the new lines. + is the set of tokens on the patchs added lines. Removed and context lines can be copied from ctx(z), so scoring them mostly rewards the edited file is shown. cost for size and requests. Without cost, the best localization is show everything. tok(zk) is the size of the localized code and ak the number of extra reads the fixer needs. target effective sample size. Raw score gaps make the weights one-hot. We choose τ per task so that the effective sample size is n: = 2 (soft EM) keeps about two candidates; = 1 (hard EM) keeps the best one. Both penalties are set to 0.25 σ, where σ = 0.068 nats per token is the median spread of scores within task. 3 Figure 2: One round of FGL. The localizer proposes candidate localizations; frozen fixer scores each by its likelihood of the verified patch y; the normalized scores weight ordinary fine-tuning of the localizer. No tests run and no reinforcement learning is used.

sections.title: 2.4 Training
sections.content: The localizer loss is weighted negative log-likelihood of the candidates plus an anchor on the teachers own localization zteacher with weight β = 0.5: Lloc(ϕ) = (cid:88) (cid:88) wik log pϕ(zik xi, Ri) β log pϕ (cid:0)zteacher xi, Ri (cid:1). (4) (cid:88) 1. Two folds. We split the training tasks into two halves, fold and fold B, and train one localizer and one fixer on each half. These fold models are used only to propose and score candidates; they are never deployed. The reason is memorization. fixer that was trained on tasks patch can reproduce that patch from almost any context, so every candidate would get high score and the weights would carry no information. In the same way, localizer trained on task mostly repeats the teachers answer, so there would be little to choose from. Using the other folds models avoids both problems: every task is handled only by models that never saw it. 2. Candidates. For each task, the localizer of the other fold proposes = 8 localizations (temperature 0.8). We add the teachers localization zteacher and few simple variants (only the edited code, only the viewed code, the teachers answer minus one item). After removing duplicates, task has 7.1 candidates on average. 3. Scores. The fixer of the other fold reads each candidate and gives the score sk of eq. (3): the average logprobability of the patchs new lines, minus the costs for size and requests. This is one forward pass per candidate, with no gradient and no test run. 4 Figure 3: Where the training signal comes from. Top: reinforcement learning runs every sampled patch against tests in sandbox. Bottom: FGL scores each localization with one forward pass of the frozen fixer over the verified patch and trains with weighted fine-tuning. 4. Weights. The scores become weights wk with the per-task temperature of the previous section. For each task we keep the three candidates with the highest weight and add the teachers localization as an anchor with weight β = 0.5, so the localizer does not drift too far from it. The weights of task sum to one. 5. Fine-tuning. The deployed localizer, trained on all tasks, is fine-tuned on these weighted candidates with the loss of eq. (4), starting from its previous version at half the learning rate. This is ordinary weighted supervised fine-tuning: there are no online rollouts and no test runs (Figure 3). The full method also retrains the fixer on the new localizations in alternation with the localizer. In this paper we run one round and update only the localizer; every two-agent system uses the same fixer.

sections.title: 4 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Model and training. All adapters are trained on Gemma 4 E4B [Gemma Team, Google DeepMind, 2026]. The competition serves an int4 checkpoint, so we train bf16 LoRA (rank 64) on dequantized copy and serve the adapter unmerged on the int4 model, as the scorer does; log-probabilities differ by 0.03 nats per token between training and serving. Each model is trained for about 250 optimizer steps of 16 sequences of up to 32,768 tokens, at learning rate 2 104 (half for warm starts). Settings are in appendix B. Systems. Base: the untrained model as single agent. S1: one adapter trained on the full teacher trajectories. S2a / S2a-view: localizer and fixer trained separately; the localizer learns the edited code (S2a) or the viewed code (S2a-view). S2b: as S2a, with the fixer also trained on imperfect localizations and requests. This is the fixer for every Stage 3 system. S3r0: localizer trained on the teachers localization (edited and viewed code). S3r1-soft / S3r1-hard: S3r0 plus one EM round with = 2 or 1. S3r1-ctrl: S3r0 plus the same extra training on the teachers localization only. Soft against ctrl isolates the effect of the EM targets. Stage 3 as run. Stage 3 uses three kinds of localizer and fixer. (1) Fold models: we split the training tasks into two halves, and B, and train one localizer and one fixer on each half (the fixers with the S2b recipe). (2) S3r0 : localizer trained on all tasks with the teachers localization (s3_loc_r0). (3) The S2b fixer, trained on all tasks. For every task, the localizer of the other half proposes = 8 answers (temperature 0.8); we add the teachers localization and few simple variants, which gives 7.1 different candidates per task on average. The fixer of the other half then scores every candidate. One of the four scoring jobs stopped early, so 1,040 of the tasks have scores; the other tasks keep only the teachers localization in Round 1. S3r1-soft and S3r1-hard are S3r0 fine-tuned on these weighted candidates; S3r1-ctrl is S3r0 fine-tuned on the teachers localization again. The fold models only propose and score; at evaluation, every S3 localizer works with the S2b fixer. Evaluation. We use the 78 development tasks whose reference fix passes its tests in our Kaggle environment (of 129). Each run uses the competition harness on 4L4 GPUs (vLLM, tensor parallel 4), 8 minutes https://huggingface.co/Hennara/locfix-e4b-runs_p 8 per task, 36 tool calls for one agent and 44 for two, and 4 tasks in parallel. task is solved when its hidden tests pass. Runs used two sampling settings: temperature 0.2-0.3 with an 8,192-token output limit, and temperature 0.7 with 6,656. We compare systems only within setting, with the exact McNemar test [McNemar, 1947] on the same tasks.

sections.title: 5.1 Offline: the EM target helps the fixer as much, with less code
sections.content: Before training on the EM targets we ran an offline check on 1,016 training tasks. For each task, the other folds fixer ran live from two inputs: the teachers localization (T) or the highest-weight candidate (S). We then compared where it edited with the verified patch  (Table 3)  . The two inputs are equally useful: the first edit lands at patched location in 43.1% of attempts with and 42.4% with (p = 0.74). But is 27.5% smaller and causes 44% fewer context overflows. The fixer also prefers candidate other than the teachers on 83% of tasks, and on 86% even without the size penalty; most often it prefers the localizers own proposals (43%) or the edited functions alone (26%). Writing the exact verified patch is too rare at this model size (1%) to compare.

sections.title: 5.3 What limits a 4B agent here
sections.content: The trace of every run lets us see where the 8 minutes go. Four problems explain most failures. 1. Trained agents explore, then run out of time. The base model makes median of 11 tool calls, finishes in about 2.5 minutes and submits guess: 61 of 78 tasks end with patch that fails the tests. Every trained system makes about three times as many calls (30-44) and makes far fewer wrong patches (9-14 at low temperature). But 54-60 of 78 tasks then run out of budget. The teacher needed median of 15 calls within the same 8 minutes, on fast API. On 4L4, with 4 tasks in parallel, the student generates about 50 tokens per second per task, so it imitates pace it cannot keep. The scorer runs one task at time, so our timeout counts are pessimistic, but the gap is large. 10 2. Low temperature causes repetition loops. At temperature 0.2-0.3, 1335 tasks per run contain an output that repeats one line until the output limit; each such output costs 130-150 seconds, more than quarter of the budget. Two-agent systems loop about twice as often as S1 (28-35 tasks against 13-18). At temperature 0.6-0.7, loops drop to 10-16 tasks for every system. Only 16 of 222 looping outputs in the two-agent runs contain one of our fixed sentences, so the fixed text is not the main cause. 3. Temperature trades timeouts for wrong patches. Moving S1 from 0.2 to 0.6 cuts the out-of-budget tasks from 54-56 to 24, but wrong patches rise from 9-14 to 40, and solved tasks do not rise. The same holds for the two-agent systems (out of budget 54-60 32-38; wrong patches 1014 2531). Once the agent has time, the next limit is the quality of its edits. 4. The trained localizers assume code layout. Every two-agent system uses paths under /workspace/src/ that do not exist in 24-43 tasks, for example in fastapi and rich, and gets five or more No such file errors in 27-54 tasks. S1 does this in 6 and 2-7 tasks. The localizers keep the assumption even after listing the repository. The S3 localizers do it less than the S2 ones at the same settings (24-35 against 41-43 tasks), which fits the offline finding that the EM target is closer to what the fixer needs.

sections.title: 6 Discussion
sections.content: Why the offline gain does not become more solved tasks. The signal test and the EM scores measure whether the fixer is looking at the right code. At E4B scale, most tasks fail later: the agent runs out of time, loops, or writes wrong edit (Section 5.3). better localizer cannot fix these. The EM round did improve what it can affect, reaching patch and wasting fewer reads, which suggests the method is sound and the bottleneck is elsewhere for 4B model. Lessons for others. Match the teachers pace to the students hardware. trajectory that fits in 8 minutes on fast API does not fit on 4L4. Filter or shorten trajectories by the students expected time, not the teachers. Leave room in the context window. The harness asks for up to 16,384 output tokens with 32K window, so any prompt above 16K tokens is rejected; in our first run this ended 4 of 5 tasks. An output limit of 6-8K avoids it. On this serving path the thinking budget was not enforced: outputs reached the full limit with 1,536-token budget. Run small evaluations more than once. On 78 tasks the same model varies by three solved tasks; report paired tests and the set of solved tasks, not only the rate.

sections.title: 7 Limitations
sections.content: We trained one model size (E4B) and ran one EM round that updated only the localizer. Each setting was run once per system, and the two groups of runs use different sampling settings, so we compare only within group. We evaluated 4 tasks in parallel, which is slower per task than the scorer. The signal test measures where the fixer edits, not whether its patch passes. Candidate localizations were sampled after the teachers exploration, not after the localizers own.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: We proposed Fixer-Guided Localization, which trains code localizer on what makes verified patch likely under the fixer, using only weighted supervised fine-tuning. Offline, its target helps the fixer as much as the teachers localization with 27.5% less code; end to end on Gemma 4 E4B it moves the agent the right way (more patches, fewer wasted reads) but the gain in solved tasks is not significant. Our analysis of 13 runs shows that, for 4B model under an 8-minute budget on 4L4, time, repetition loops and edit quality limit the agent more than localization does. We release the 1,629 verified trajectories, the data and training code, and all trained adapters. Larger models, further EM rounds and fixer updates are left to follow-up paper.

sections.title: A Harness Facts that Shape Training
sections.content: Table 5: Behaviour of the competition harness (swegemma 0.2.11, adk_submission 0.2.13, adk_eval_core 0.1.0, google-adk 1.39.1), verified from the wheels and on Kaggle, and its consequence for training. Fact Consequence for training not run_command, read_file, counted: The whole trajectory renders as one model turn; tool calls and results are special-token spans inside it. Thinking is shown only for assistant messages with tool calls after the last user message. Visible text on tool-call message renders after the tool responses. ADK appends You are an agent. Your internal name is . . . to the system prompt. Counted tools: edit_file, write_file; get_status, submit_patch. budget warning is appended to tool response when 10 or fewer calls remain (budget at least 20). The time budget is hard timeout; afterwards the current diff is graded. interval 15, overlap 2, threshold Compaction: 14,336 tokens, retention 5; the root agent writes the summary. read_file: at most 150 lines and 10,000 characters, cut mid-line at the character cap while end_line reports the line cap. run_command: 5,000 characters; 300 timeout. sub-agent tool returns {"result": "<final non-thought text>"}. true ends the fixers skip_summarization: turn after the localizer call and triggers nudge. LoRA modules: 258 on E4B (KV-shared layers have no k/v projections). E4B on 4L4: 298,464 tokens of KV cache. stdout and stderr each cut at Training text is built from the exact messages the client sends, rendered with the models own chat template. Records are cut into segments at every new user message. Teacher narration on tool-call turns is folded into the thinking channel. Replay routes each request to the right agents script by this line. Budget messages are rewritten per counted call. Re-generated with the harnesss own function for the training budget. cut-off run can still score if it edited early. Contexts above about 14K tokens are summarized at inference; no compaction inside the localizer. Synthetic reads are chunked so every output is complete. Used when rebuilding code from traces. Fixer records contain exactly this wrapper. The localizer tool uses skip_summarization: false. Adapters cover only the projections that exist. Several full 32K sessions fit at once.

sections.title: F Reproduction
sections.content: Every step runs through one command-line tool; each command takes configuration file and overrides, and writes its resolved configuration, git commit and package versions next to its output. The code is split into two repositories: Data (https://github.com/khalil-Hennara/codeagent-validate): task ingest and validation, teacher runs and grading, recall cleaning, trace statistics and budget sweeps, base-commit code fetch, and single-agent and two-agent record building in parallel shards, with merge, schema check and the task-level validation split. Training (https://github.com/misraj-ai/locfix): dequantization once per model; GPU smoke test (dequantize, parity, overfit, export, parity, generation); dry-run training plan; training; and parity check of the exported adapter before any evaluation. Stage 3 adds the fold split (em.fold-split), candidate generation (em.candidates), scoring sequences (score.prepare), scoring (score.run), weights (score.weights), the offline signal test (em.signal-test) and the Round-1 records (em.r1-records); submit.package builds and checks the submissions. Versions: vLLM 0.19.1 (competition build), transformers 5.13.1, peft 0.21.2, accelerate 1.15.0, compressed-tensors 0.15.0.1, google-adk 1.39.1, litellm 1.106.3, Python 3.12 (training).
